prompt.context: Your client, Donald Drumpf, is a 70-year-old real estate mogul who inherited his wealth from his late father. Drumpf Enterprises primarily operates within the real estate/hospitality industry with numerous high-end Drumpf hotels (50% of overall top-line revenue) and golf courses located worldwide. Lately, Drumpf has seen shrinking per-room profit margins for his hotel business. He believes the shrinking margins are due to increased competition from AirBnB and similar businesses. In order to diversify his portfolio, he intends to enter the airline industry and 'Make Airlines Great Again' by leveraging his success in hospitality to create an airline that offers first-class comforts. Donald Drumpf wants to enter this industry quickly and has identified 2 airlines to consider. He believes either airline would help increase the overall profit margin of his business. Donald Drumpf has hired you to help with this matter. Despite Drumpf being convinced about airlines, the partner at your firm leading this engagement thinks the team needs to look at the hotel business' profitability as well.
prompt.question: How should Drumpf address the decline in hotel profitability, and should he acquire one of the two identified airlines to increase overall profit margins?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current profit margin of the hotel business?
clarifying_info.a: Current hotel business profit margin is 14%.
Increase overall profitability for Drumpf Enterprises.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have overall revenue and cost breakouts for the hotel business?
clarifying_info.a: We do not have an overall breakout for the entire business; rather we have metrics per room.

clarifying_info.q: What is the tax rate for the DCF?

exhibits.title: Hotel Room Revenue/Cost Metrics & Competitive Pricing Information
exhibits.shows: Two charts: (1) a bar chart showing Drumpf's average price per room and average cost per room per night from 2012 to 2016; (2) a line chart comparing average price per room from 2012 to 2018 across four hotel chains (Sparriott, Drumpf, Staroak, Bilton). A note states price elasticity of demand is -2.0.

exhibits.title: Drumpf Hotel Cost Trend & Competitor Cost Benchmark (per $100 room revenue)
exhibits.shows: Two stacked-bar charts: (1) Drumpf's cost breakdown per $100 room revenue for 2014, 2015, and 2016, broken into Salaries, SG&A, Advertising, Overhead, and Profit; (2) Competitor 2016 cost breakdown per $100 room revenue for Bilton, Drumpf, Staroak, and Sparriott using the same categories. Note: figures exclude costs for purchasing and developing new hotels.

exhibits.title: Hotel Specific Metrics
exhibits.shows: A detailed comparison table of hotel-specific metrics across Drumpf, Bilton, Sparriott, and Staroak, including number of hotels worldwide, new hotels opened in the past 2 years, locations of new hotels, average rooms per hotel (2014 and 2016), average employees per hotel (2014 and 2016), amenities, maid service frequency, average time to service a room, average occupancy rate, types of bed offered, and average salary per employee.

exhibits.title: Income Statements for GTHC Airlines and Tarheel Airways
exhibits.shows: Income statements for the last fiscal year for two airlines: GTHC Airlines and Tarheel Airways, including revenue, cost line items, EBIT, depreciation, capital expenditures, and net income figures (in $M).

Tarheel.note: No capital expenditures listed; additional renovation costs estimated at $5B to upgrade fleet

framework: Drumpf Economics — Current Business: analyze hotel revenue streams (room revenue, restaurant, golf) and cost structure (salaries, upkeep/renovation, fixed assets)
Drumpf Economics — New Business: analyze potential airline revenue (tickets, fees, baggage) and acquisition/renovation costs
Strategic Considerations — Competition: what are competitor hotels doing; are they experiencing declining profits too?
Strategic Considerations — Economy: is there a broader economic slowdown driving lower demand?
Strategic Considerations — Financing: can Drumpf finance an acquisition of this scale?
Strategic Considerations — Strategy/Fit: why airlines? what else could be done? core competency is not airlines.
Strategic Considerations — Risks: no airline operating experience; huge financial exposure; synergies uncertain
Lead with the core business first: the prompt is designed to mislead the candidate toward the airline. A strong candidate diagnoses the hotel profitability decline before evaluating an acquisition.

questions.prompt: What is driving the decline in hotel profit margins? Use Exhibit 1.
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: (1) costs are rising faster than prices — average cost per room rose from $162 (2012) to $215 (2016) while price rose from $205 to $250; (2) Drumpf is priced approximately 26% higher than competitors (~$250 vs ~$198), which may be limiting demand. CAGR of profit margin 2012-2016: (35-43)^0.25 - 1 = -5%. Do not make the candidate calculate CAGR but ask if they know the formula, then provide the result.

math.setup: Profit margin CAGR = (ending margin / beginning margin)^(1/years) - 1
steps: Profit margin 2012 = 43% (per Exhibit 2 extrapolated) vs 2016 = 14%? Note: Exhibit 1 shows profit per room declining relative to price. Exhibit 2 shows Drumpf profit at 14% in 2016 and approximately 20% in 2014, implying decline.
math.answer: Profit margin declining at approximately -5% CAGR 2012-2016; driven by costs rising faster than revenue

questions.prompt: What specific cost is driving up expenses? Use Exhibit 2.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify salaries as the main driver. Salaries rose from 37% of room revenue in 2014 to 43% in 2016 — a 6 percentage-point increase (16.2% relative increase). Drumpf salaries are approximately 8% higher per $100 of room revenue than competitors (who average ~35%). Candidate should ask why salaries increased and brainstorm reasons before receiving Exhibit 3.

math.setup: Compare Drumpf salaries % across years and vs competitors
steps: Drumpf 2016 salary share: 43%; nearest competitor (Bilton) 22% — Drumpf is ~21 pp higher than Bilton, and ~8 pp higher than Staroak (35%)
math.answer: Salaries expense rose by ~$28/room (from ~$80 to ~$108), a ~35% increase, and Drumpf salaries are ~8 pp higher per $100 of revenue than the average competitor

questions.prompt: Why might salaries be so high and increasing? What does Exhibit 3 tell us?
questions.guidance: Candidate should focus on: (1) employees per room ratio — Drumpf went from 1 employee per 6 rooms (2014) to 1 per 4 rooms (2016), while competitors stayed at roughly 1 per 6 rooms; (2) average service time — Drumpf takes 40 minutes vs ~30 minutes for competitors, likely due to rapid expansion (10 new hotels in 2 years = 25% of total hotels, all in high-cost countries) creating untrained staff; (3) the solution is better training to bring service time to 30 minutes and laying off excess employees to restore a 1:6 employee-to-room ratio. Candidate should also note potential revenue upside from using price elasticity of demand.

math.setup: Calculate employees to lay off and salary savings; also calculate revenue impact of price reduction
steps: Target ratio: 1 employee per 6 rooms. Drumpf has 600 rooms/hotel, so target = 100 employees/hotel. Current = 150. Excess = 50 employees per hotel.
Revenue impact of 10% price cut (using elasticity of -2.0): price drops by $25 (10% of $250) -> demand increases by 20%
math.answer: Laying off excess employees saves $100M; reducing room price by 10% increases annual revenue by $151.2M; combined benefit $251.2M

questions.prompt: By how much can Drumpf increase profits for his hotel business? (Prompt #2 — assume hotel room revenue is the only revenue.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should combine the two improvement levers: labor cost savings and revenue increase from price reduction. Total potential increase in profit = $100M + $151.2M = $251.2M. Candidate may optionally calculate new profit margin: reducing salaries by 33% (150->100 employees) cuts salary share by ~14.3 pp, raising margin from 14% to ~28.3% at $250 price; at $225 price, profit per room = $225 - $180 (costs) = $45, margin ~20%, still higher than current 14%.

math.setup: Total hotel room revenue = Avg price * Avg rooms * Occupancy * Hotels * 360 days
steps: Savings from labor reduction = 50 employees/hotel * 50 hotels * $40,000 = $100M
New revenue at $225 price and 25,200 rooms/day = $225 * 25,200 * 360 = $2.0412B
math.answer: Total potential increase in profit: $251.2M ($100M from labor savings + $151.2M from price-driven revenue growth)

questions.prompt: Evaluate the two airline acquisition options using the DCF figures in Exhibit 4.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate free cash flow for each airline as EBIT*(1-tax rate) + Depreciation - Change in NWC - CapEx, then divide by (discount rate - growth rate) for terminal value. Tarheel: higher operating margin (14%) but $25.2B valuation and $5B additional costs. GTHC: lower operating margin (8%) but higher net income margin (26% due to asset gains), $14.6B valuation, only $1.5B additional costs. There is no single correct airline to pick; key insight is that neither acquisition is realistic given Drumpf's ~$3.8B annual top-line revenue. Challenge candidate on financing, core competency, and whether airlines solve the profitability problem at all.

math.setup: FCF = EBIT*(1-Tax Rate) - CapEx; Valuation = FCF / (Discount Rate - Growth Rate)
steps: Tarheel FCF: EBIT=3600, Tax=1080, EBIT*(1-0.30)=2520, No CapEx listed -> FCF=2520
GTHC FCF: EBIT=2800, Tax=840, EBIT*(1-0.30)=1960; but note EBIT-Tax=2800-840=1960... casebook states EBIT-Tax=1560 implying depreciation or other adj; after CapEx: 1560-100=1460
Tarheel Operating Margin=14%, Net Income Margin=20%; GTHC Operating Margin=8%, Net Income Margin=26% (inflated by gain on asset sales)
Additional costs: Tarheel $5B (new aircraft leases), GTHC $1.5B (renovations)
math.answer: Tarheel valued at ~$25.2B + $5B additional costs; GTHC valued at ~$14.6B + $1.5B additional costs. Neither acquisition is realistic versus Drumpf's ~$3.8B annual revenue.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might Drumpf hotels have higher salaries or an increasing number of employees per room?

categories.name: Rapid Expansion / New Hotel Openings
ideas: 10 new hotels opened in past 2 years (25% of total portfolio)
New hotel staff have lower efficiency due to lack of training and familiarity
Learning curve means service time is higher (40 min vs 30 min for competitors)

categories.name: Location of New Hotels
ideas: All 10 new Drumpf hotels are in high-cost labor countries (US, England, Switzerland, France)
Competitor new hotels are mostly in lower-cost labor markets (India, Peru, Belarus, Colombia, Argentina, Madagascar)

categories.name: Service Standards & Amenities
ideas: Drumpf offers more premium amenities (heated floors, marble bathrooms, spa) requiring more specialized staff
Premium service standards may require higher staff-to-room ratios

categories.name: Operational Inefficiency
ideas: Lack of standardized training program across hotels
No systematic efficiency benchmarking against competitors

recommendation: Do NOT acquire an airline at this time — the core hotel profitability problem can be solved through internal operational improvements that are far less costly and within Drumpf's area of expertise

Implement two immediate hotel improvement levers: (1) improve housekeeping training to reduce average room service time from 40 to 30 minutes, enabling reduction of excess staff (50 employees/hotel), saving $100M annually; (2) consider a 10% price reduction to leverage price elasticity of -2.0 to grow occupied rooms from 21,000 to 25,200/day, adding $151.2M in annual revenue
Combined impact: $251.2M increase in annual profit, meaningfully reversing the margin decline without a multi-billion-dollar acquisition

If diversification is still desired after fixing the core business, a smaller or more synergistic investment (e.g., travel-adjacent services) would be more appropriate than a $15B-$25B airline acquisition
risks: Internal backlash and morale impact from laying off approximately 2,500 employees (50 per hotel)
Potential decline in service quality if staff reductions are not managed carefully
Lowering hotel prices could trigger a competitive price war; competitors may respond with their own price cuts
Reducing prices may damage the Drumpf premium brand image and attract a different customer segment
If an airline is acquired: significant financing risk, no airline operating experience, culture clashes, uncertain synergies between hospitality and aviation
next_steps: Identify which hotels have the highest average room service times and design a targeted training program for housekeeping
Conduct a competitive analysis to model competitor response to a 10% price decrease before implementing
Run a pilot price reduction at 2-3 hotels to test demand elasticity in practice before rolling out system-wide
Engage HR and legal to plan any workforce restructuring with appropriate notice periods and retention of top performers
